吴承恩: Wu Cheng'en (c. 1500?1582) was a Ming-dynasty writer traditionally credited with Journey to the West, an imaginative epic of pilgrimage, faith, and rebellion.
罗贯中: Luo Guanzhong (c. 1330?1400) is traditionally regarded as the author of Romance of the Three Kingdoms, whose vast panorama of war, strategy, and loyalty shaped the Chinese historical novel.
曹雪芹: Cao Xueqin (c. 1715?1763) drew on his own family's decline in Dream of the Red Chamber, a psychologically subtle masterpiece about love and the fall of an aristocratic Qing household.
孙武: Sun Tzu, probably active in the fifth century BCE, is traditionally credited with The Art of War, whose teachings on deception, intelligence, and adaptability have influenced strategy worldwide.
老子: Laozi is the legendary sage credited with the Daodejing, a foundational Daoist text on the Way, virtue, non-action, and the return to simplicity.
孔子及其弟子: Confucius (551?479 BCE) and his disciples established an ethical tradition centered on learning, humaneness, and responsible government; their conversations are preserved in the Analects.
庄周: Zhuang Zhou (c. 369?286 BCE) was an influential Daoist thinker; the Zhuangzi uses parable, humor, and dream to explore freedom, change, and the limits of certain knowledge.
孟轲: Mencius (c. 372?289 BCE) developed Confucian thought by defending the innate goodness of human nature and the ruler's duty to govern humanely.
墨翟: Mozi (c. 470?391 BCE) taught impartial care, frugality, and opposition to aggressive war, offering a practical alternative to early Confucianism.
韩非: Han Fei (c. 280?233 BCE) systematized Legalist thought, presenting clear laws, administrative technique, and institutional authority as the foundations of a strong state.
列御寇: Lie Yukou is a possibly legendary Daoist sage credited with the Liezi, a lively collection of stories about naturalness, relativity, and spiritual freedom.
佚名: This catalog label covers works whose authorship is unknown or uncertain; their anonymous voices preserve traditions shaped across many generations.
刘安: Liu An (c. 179?122 BCE), king of Huainan and patron of scholars, oversaw the Huainanzi, an encyclopedic synthesis of Daoism, cosmology, and statecraft.
鬼谷子: Guiguzi is a semi-legendary thinker of the Warring States period associated with strategic diplomacy; the text bearing his name examines persuasion, psychology, and political tactics.
古籍: This attribution denotes no single author but ancient texts formed over centuries, as myths and traditions passed through unknown storytellers, scribes, and editors.
司马迁: Sima Qian (c. 145?86 BCE) wrote the Records of the Grand Historian, spanning three millennia and establishing the biographical model for later Chinese dynastic histories.
干宝: Gan Bao (d. 336) was an Eastern Jin historian who collected brief accounts of ghosts, marvels, and popular belief in In Search of the Supernatural.
鲁迅: Lu Xun (1881?1936), born Zhou Shuren, transformed modern Chinese literature through incisive social criticism; A Madman's Diary and The True Story of Ah Q became landmark works.
老舍: Lao She (1899?1966), born Shu Qingchun, was a Beijing novelist and playwright whose Rickshaw Boy portrays an ordinary man's crushed hopes with humor and compassion.
东鲁古狂生: Donglu Gukuangsheng was a Qing-dynasty writer whose satirical story collection The Drunken Awakening Stone exposed social vice, judicial corruption, and moral decay through lively vernacular tales.
公孙龙: Gongsun Long (c. 320–250 BCE) was a Warring States logician of the School of Names, famous for his 'White Horse is Not a Horse' paradox and treatises examining the relationship between language and reality.
冯梦龙: Feng Menglong (1574–1646) was a late Ming vernacular literary master whose 'Three Words' anthologies, including Stories to Enlighten the World, transformed urban popular culture into immortal classic fiction.
刘劭: Liu Shao (c. 168–245) was a Three Kingdoms thinker and Wei official whose treatise Study of Human Abilities pioneered the systematic evaluation of human character, talent, and leadership.
刘勰: Liu Xie (c. 465–522) was a Southern Dynasties literary theorist whose masterpiece The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons stands as China's greatest systematic treatise on aesthetics and criticism.
刘向: Liu Xiang (77–6 BCE) was a Western Han Confucian scholar and imperial bibliographer who compiled Garden of Stories and New Prefaces, preserving early moral parables and historical lore.
刘基: Liu Ji (1311–1375), known as Liu Bowen, was a founding strategist of the Ming Dynasty, poet, and philosopher whose allegorical work Yulizi offers profound fables on statecraft and human folly.
刘歆: Liu Xin (c. 50 BCE – 23 CE) was a Western Han polymath, astronomer, and bibliographer attributed with Miscellanies of the Western Capital, chronicling court life and marvels in the Han capital.
刘璋: Liu Zhang (1667–?) was a Qing-dynasty novelist and satirist whose novel The Slaying of the Ghosts exposed earthly vices, corruption, and social hypocrisies through Zhong Kui's underworld battles.
刘鹗: Liu E (1857–1909) was a late Qing scholar and reformer whose novel The Travels of Lao Can used an itinerant doctor's wanderings to expose judicial cruelty and mourn a crumbling dynasty.
半云友: Ban Yunyou was a Qing-dynasty author of romantic fiction whose novel The Phoenix Flute celebrated talent, virtue, and faithful love amid the conventions of the scholar-and-beauty tradition.
吕尚: Lü Shang (Jiang Ziya, 11th c. BCE) was the chief military advisor who helped King Wen and King Wu overthrow the Shang Dynasty; he is traditionally credited with the strategic classic Six Secret Teachings.
吕生: Lü Sheng was a Qing-dynasty writer whose allegorical novel A Fool's Dream Talk satirized greed, official ambition, and human vanity through the surreal structure of an illusionary dream journey.
吴敬梓: Wu Jingzi (1701–1754) was a Qing-dynasty scholar-author whose monumental satirical novel The Scholars mercilessly exposed the corruption, hypocrisy, and hollow vanity of the imperial examination system.
吴楚材、吴调侯: Wu Chucai and Wu Tiaohou were Qing-dynasty scholars and educators who compiled Guwen Guanzhi, the most revered and enduring anthology of classical Chinese prose spanning two millennia.
周兴嗣: Zhou Xingsi (c. 469–521) was a Liang-dynasty court scholar who composed the Thousand Character Classic overnight by imperial order, using exactly one thousand unique characters in four-character rhyming verses.
商鞅: Shang Yang (c. 390–338 BCE) was a Warring States Legalist statesman whose radical reforms transformed Qin into a formidable military state; his governance philosophy is compiled in The Book of Lord Shang.
天花藏主人: Tianhuazang Zhuren was the pen name of an influential 17th-century novelist who perfected the scholar-and-beauty romance genre, best known for the internationally translated classic Yu Jiao Li.
子思: Zisi (Kong Ji, c. 483–402 BCE) was the grandson of Confucius and teacher of Mencius's mentors; he is credited with The Doctrine of the Mean, which explores universal harmony and sincerity in moral life.
尉缭: Wei Liao was a 4th-century BCE Warring States military strategist who advised King Zheng of Qin; his treatise Wei Liaozi integrates political ethics, strict discipline, and psychological warfare.
尹文: Yin Wen (c. 360–280 BCE) was a Warring States philosopher of the Jixia Academy whose treatise Yin Wenzi synthesized Daoist naturalness and Legalist regulation to propose pragmatic and just governance.
左丘明: Zuo Qiuming (c. 502–422 BCE) was a Spring and Autumn period historian and official court scribe of Lu, traditionally revered as the compiler of Discourses of the States and the Zuo Commentary.
张拟: Zhang Ni was an 11th-century Northern Song scholar and master of Go who wrote The Classic of Go (Thirteen Chapters), codifying the deep strategic, psychological, and tactical principles of Weiqi.
张潮: Zhang Chao (1650–?) was a Qing-dynasty essayist, calligrapher, and aesthetic connoisseur whose aphoristic masterpiece Quiet Dream Shadows celebrates art, friendship, nature, and the cultured soul.
张鷟: Zhang Zhuo (c. 660–740) was a Tang-dynasty scholar-official whose vivid notebook Anecdotes from Court and Country preserved colorful court intrigues, supernatural wonders, and folk humor of the early Tang.
徐霞客: Xu Xiake (1587–1641) was a Ming-dynasty explorer and literary stylist whose monumental Travel Diaries documented thirty years of intrepid scientific exploration across China's wild landscapes.
惠能: Huineng (638–713) was the revered Sixth Patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism whose teachings on sudden enlightenment and inherent Buddha-nature are preserved in the seminal Platform Sutra.
施耐庵: Shi Nai'an (c. 1296–1372) was a Yuan-Ming writer traditionally credited with Water Margin, one of the Four Great Classical Novels celebrating the chivalric brotherhood of 108 outlaw heroes at Mount Liang.
曾子: Zengzi (Zeng Shen, 505–435 BCE) was a devoted disciple of Confucius renowned for filial piety; he is credited with The Great Learning, articulating self-cultivation as the foundation of world peace.
朱柏庐: Zhu Bailu (1627–1698) was a Ming-Qing Neo-Confucian educator whose household maxims Zhu's Family Instructions became the classic Chinese guide for domestic discipline, frugality, and personal integrity.
朱熹、吕祖谦: Zhu Xi (1130–1200) and Lü Zuqian (1137–1181) were leading Song Neo-Confucian philosophers who compiled Reflections on Things at Hand, establishing the comprehensive curriculum of Neo-Confucianism.
李宝嘉: Li Baojia (Li Boyuan, 1867–1906) was a late Qing journalist and satirical novelist whose work Officialdom Unmasked vividly cataloged bureaucratic venality and moral decay during China's transition.
李毓秀: Li Yuxiu (1662–1722) was a Qing-dynasty Confucian educator who composed Standards for Students (Dizigui), a widely recited primer instilling filial respect, honesty, and brotherly affection in youth.
李汝珍: Li Ruzhen (c. 1763–1830) was a Qing-dynasty polymath, phonologist, and novelist whose fantasy masterpiece Flowers in the Mirror blended mythical voyages, linguistic wit, and early feminist ideals.
李渔: Li Yu (1611–1680), known as Liweng, was an ingenious playwright, novelist, and essayist whose Casual Expressions of Idle Feeling and romantic plays celebrated joyful living, theatre, and design.
汤显祖: Tang Xianzu (1550–1616) was the preeminent dramatist of the Ming Dynasty, often hailed as China's Shakespeare; his immortal Kunqu masterpiece The Peony Pavilion elevated romantic love to a cosmic, redemptive force.
沈括: Shen Kuo (1031–1095) was a Northern Song polymath, astronomer, and statesman whose encyclopedic Dream Pool Essays recorded world-first observations in magnetism, astronomy, printing, and geology.
熊大木: Xiong Damu was a 16th-century Ming-dynasty novelist and book publisher who popularized historical epics, compiling the beloved patriotic military saga Generals of the Yang Family.
爱月主人: Aiyue Zhuren was a Qing-dynasty author of romantic drama and fiction, best known for A Play Within a Play, which wove theatre within fiction to explore destiny, virtue, and love.
王实甫: Wang Shifu (c. 1260–1336) was a Yuan-dynasty dramatist whose poetically exquisite play Romance of the Western Chamber represents the supreme achievement of Chinese romantic zaju drama.
王应麟: Wang Yinglin (1223–1296) was a Southern Song polymath, historian, and scholar traditionally credited with authoring the Three Character Classic, China's most celebrated introductory primer.
王筠: Wang Yun (1784–1854) was a Qing-dynasty philologist and paleographer who wrote Wenzi Mengqiu to introduce young students to character radicals, phonetic components, and the logic of Chinese writing.
白云道人: Baiyun Daoren was a Qing-dynasty writer whose popular novel Spring in the Jade Tower combined intricate romantic storylines with lively observations of Ming-Qing social customs.
白行简: Bai Xingjian (776–826) was a Tang-dynasty writer and official, brother of the poet Bai Juyi, famed for The Tale of Li Wa, a masterpiece of classical narrative prose exploring love across social divides.
程允升: Cheng Yunsheng was a Ming-dynasty scholar who compiled Gems of Early Learning, an encyclopedic rhyming manual of historical allusions, astronomical lore, and social etiquette for young learners.
管仲: Guan Zhong (c. 720–645 BCE) was a legendary statesman whose pragmatic administrative, economic, and military reforms made the State of Qi the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn era.
纪昀: Ji Yun (1724–1805), known as Ji Xiaolan, was chief editor of the imperial Siku Quanshu; his collection Notes from the Thatched Hut for Examining Subtleties used supernatural parables to critique hypocrisy.
艾衲居士: Aina Jushi was an early Qing-dynasty author whose satirical story cycle Idle Talk Under the Bean Arbor used a conversational village setting to skewer human pretension and political moralizing.
苏曼殊: Su Manshu (1884–1918) was a late Qing and early Republican poet, Buddhist monk, painter, and translator whose autobiographical novel The Lone Swan became an icon of romantic melancholy.
苏鹗: Su E was a late Tang-dynasty jinshi scholar whose fascinating notebook Miscellaneous Records of Duyang recorded imperial court ceremonies, exotic foreign tributes, and strange wonders of the late Tang.
荀悦: Xun Yue (148–209) was an Eastern Han historian and philosopher who advised Emperor Xian; his philosophical treatise Extended Reflections examined moral decay, legalism, and just imperial statecraft.
褚人获: Chu Renhuo (1635–?) was a Qing-dynasty novelist and scholar who synthesized history, popular drama, and legends into the sprawling martial epic Romance of the Sui and Tang.
许仲琳: Xu Zhonglin (c. 1560–1630) was a Ming-dynasty novelist traditionally credited with compiling The Investiture of the Gods, a mythical epic chronicling supernatural warfare at the fall of the Shang Dynasty.
贾谊: Jia Yi (200–168 BCE) was a Western Han statesman, orator, and poet whose incisive political essays on governance and the lessons of Qin's collapse are preserved in The New Book of Jia Yi.
车万育: Che Wanyu (1632–1705) was a Qing-dynasty scholar who created Rhyme Enlightenment, the classic rhythmic manual that taught generations of learners the tonal balance and rhymes of Chinese poetry.
邓析: Deng Xi (c. 545–501 BCE) was a Spring and Autumn period philosopher and legal pioneer of the School of Names who promulgated China's early bamboo-slip legal code and championed logical debate.
邹必显: Zou Bixian was a Qing-dynasty novelist who composed The Complete Tale of Feituo, an entertaining martial romance celebrating upright knights-errant and the triumph of virtue over lawlessness.
钟嵘: Zhong Rong (c. 468–518) was a Southern Dynasties literary critic whose pioneering work The Poets' Grading systematically evaluated five-character poetry from the Han to Liang into three qualitative tiers.
陆羽: Lu Yu (733–804) was the Tang-dynasty 'Sage of Tea' who wrote The Classic of Tea, the world's very first comprehensive monograph establishing the culture, brewing methods, and spiritual philosophy of tea.
陶渊明: Tao Yuanming (c. 365–427), also known as Tao Qian, was a beloved Six Dynasties recluse poet and author whose Further Records of Searching for Spirits documented mysterious supernatural tales.
韩婴: Han Ying (c. 200–130 BCE) was a Western Han Confucian master whose Outer Traditions of the Han School of Songs used poems from the Book of Songs to explain moral conduct and statecraft through stories.
颜之推: Yan Zhitui (531–c. 591) was a Northern and Southern Dynasties scholar whose Family Instructions of Master Yan served as the definitive manual on domestic education, scholarly ethics, and self-discipline.
黄宗羲: Huang Zongxi (1610–1695) was a late Ming and early Qing philosopher and historian whose radical manifesto Waiting for the Dawn offered a groundbreaking critique of imperial autocracy.
黄石公: Huang Shigong was a legendary Qin-dynasty hermit and master strategist traditionally credited with conveying the military classic Three Strategies to Zhang Liang, chief advisor to the Han founder.
